questions.prompt: A problem is a linear program when
options: the objective and every constraint function are affine
the objective is a squared norm and the constraints are linear
the objective is convex and the constraints are arbitrary
the decision variable is required to be a matrix
questions.explanation: A linear program has an affine objective and affine equalities and inequalities. A squared norm is a quadratic objective, which makes a quadratic program when the constraints stay affine. Convexity of the objective is the wider class, and it allows constraints that are not affine as long as the feasible set stays convex. The shape of the decision variable, vector or matrix, does not decide the class.

questions.prompt: The matrix \(Q = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) and its symmetric part define the same quadratic form. What is one off-diagonal entry of that symmetric part?
questions.explanation: The quadratic form uses \(x^T Q x = x^T((Q + Q^T)/2) x\). The cross term \(6xy\) is split equally, so each off-diagonal entry of the symmetric part is \(3\). The diagonal entries stay \(2\) and \(4\). Reporting 6 keeps the unsymmetrized upper entry. Reporting 0 uses the lower entry of \(Q\) before the split. Reporting 2 uses a diagonal entry.

questions.prompt: A convex optimization problem minimizes a convex objective over
options: a nonconvex feasible set
a finite set of integers
a convex feasible set
the complement of a ball
questions.explanation: Convexity of the problem needs both pieces: a convex objective and a convex feasible set. A nonconvex set, including the complement of a ball, can hide a local solution that is not global even when the objective is convex. A finite integer set is discrete. It is not a convex set unless it contains only one point.

questions.prompt: Which of these are quadratic programs?
options: Minimize \(x^2 + 3y\) subject to \(x + y \le 1\).
Minimize \(x + y\) subject to \(x^2 + y^2 \le 1\).
Minimize \(x^2 - 4xy + y^2\) subject to \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\).
Minimize \(\lvert x \rvert + \lvert y \rvert\) subject to \(x + y = 1\).
Minimize \(\sin x\) subject to \(x \le 2\).
questions.explanation:
A quadratic program has a quadratic objective and affine constraints. The first objective is quadratic and the inequality is affine. The third objective is quadratic, indefinite even, and the constraints are affine, so it is a quadratic program that is not convex.
• A linear objective with a disk constraint is not a quadratic program: the constraint is quadratic.
• An absolute-value objective is piecewise linear, not quadratic.
• A sine is neither quadratic nor affine.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order used to classify a smooth problem with inequality constraints.
questions.explanation: The objective's algebraic degree is the first split, because it separates linear programs, quadratic programs, and general nonlinear programs. Affine constraints are what keep a quadratic objective inside the quadratic-program class. The symmetric part is the matrix whose eigenvalues are meaningful, and it does not change the quadratic form. Convexity is the last label: it needs a positive semidefinite Hessian everywhere it is used, and a convex feasible set. Testing eigenvalues before symmetrizing reads a matrix the form does not determine.

steps: Check whether the objective is affine, quadratic, or neither.
Check whether every constraint function is affine.
If the objective is quadratic, replace its matrix by the symmetric part before any eigenvalue test.
Decide convexity from that Hessian on the feasible set, together with convexity of the set.

questions.prompt: Replacing a square matrix \(Q\) by \((Q + Q^T)/2\) does not change the quadratic form because
options: \(x^T Q x = x^T ((Q + Q^T)/2) x\) for every \(x\)
the off-diagonal entries of \(Q\) never enter \(x^T Q x\)
every square matrix is already symmetric
the eigenvalues of \(Q\) and of \(Q^T\) differ by a sign
questions.explanation: The skew part \((Q - Q^T)/2\) contributes nothing to \(x^T Q x\), so the symmetric part carries the whole form. Off-diagonal entries do enter, through the cross terms, which is why they are averaged rather than dropped. A general square matrix is not symmetric. \(Q\) and \(Q^T\) have the same eigenvalues, not opposite ones.

questions.prompt: The form \(a x^2 + b xy + c y^2\) comes from a symmetric \(2 \times 2\) matrix. Write the determinant of that matrix as an expression in a, b, and c.
questions.explanation:
The symmetric matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} a & b/2 \\ b/2 & c \end{bmatrix}\), because the cross term \(bxy\) is split across the two off-diagonal entries. Its determinant is \(ac - (b/2)^2 = ac - b^2/4\).
• \(ac - b^2\) forgets to halve the cross term before squaring.
• \(a + c\) is the trace, not the determinant.
• \(ac - b/2\) subtracts the off-diagonal entry instead of its square.

questions.prompt: The objective \(\tfrac12 x^T A x\) has \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\). What is the smaller eigenvalue of the Hessian?
questions.explanation: With the factor one half and a symmetric \(A\), the Hessian is \(A\). The trace is 8 and the determinant is \(16 - 4 = 12\), so the eigenvalues sum to 8 and multiply to 12. They are 6 and 2. The smaller one is 2, which is positive, so this quadratic is strictly convex. Reporting 6 gives the larger eigenvalue. Reporting 4 gives a diagonal entry. Reporting 12 gives the determinant.

questions.prompt: A note claims that minimizing \(x^2 - y^2\) over the unit disk is a convex program. Exactly one step is false.
questions.explanation: The objective is quadratic, the unit disk is convex, and a convex objective on a convex set really is a convex program. The false step is the Hessian claim. The Hessian is \(\operatorname{diag}(2, -2)\), which has a negative eigenvalue, so the objective is not convex. The problem is a nonconvex quadratic over a convex set.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>axis-aligned ellipse</title><line x1="28" y1="104" x2="256" y2="104"/><polygon points="256,104 249.6,106.7 249.6,101.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="140" y1="186" x2="140" y2="24"/><polygon points="140,24 142.7,30.4 137.3,30.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="120" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="148" y="20" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><ellipse cx="140" cy="104" rx="86" ry="46"/><line x1="54" y1="104" x2="226" y2="104" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="140" y1="58" x2="140" y2="150" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: An ellipse centered at the origin, longer along the first axis.
steps: The objective \(x^2 - y^2\) is a quadratic function.
The unit disk is a convex set.
The Hessian of \(x^2 - y^2\) is positive semidefinite at every point.
A convex objective on a convex set defines a convex program.
reasons: The Hessian has eigenvalues 2 and -2, so it is not positive semidefinite.
The unit disk is not a convex set.

questions.prompt: You can recognize a linear program because
options: the objective is a squared residual and the constraints are bounds
the feasible set is a ball
both the objective and the constraints are affine
the Hessian is positive definite and the constraints are linear
questions.explanation: Affine data on both the objective and the constraints is the linear-program pattern. A squared residual is a quadratic objective. A ball is a quadratic constraint. A positive definite Hessian with linear constraints is a convex quadratic program, which includes linear programs only in the special case of a zero Hessian.

questions.prompt: A quadratic objective has Hessian \(P = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ 1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\). What is the smaller eigenvalue of \(P\)?
questions.explanation: The trace is 10 and the determinant is \(25 - 1 = 24\), so the eigenvalues are the roots of \(\lambda^2 - 10\lambda + 24 = 0\), which factors as \((\lambda - 4)(\lambda - 6) = 0\). The smaller eigenvalue is 4. It is positive, so \(P\) is positive definite and the quadratic is strictly convex. Reporting 6 gives the larger eigenvalue. Reporting 5 gives a diagonal entry. Reporting 1 gives an off-diagonal entry.

options: is always unbounded below
is a linear program
has a positive semidefinite Hessian
can have a local minimizer that is not global
questions.explanation: An indefinite quadratic can bend up in one direction and down in another, so a point that is best in a neighborhood need not be best on the whole feasible set. The Hessian of a nonconvex quadratic is not positive semidefinite. The objective is not affine, so the problem is not a linear program. A nonconvex quadratic can still be bounded below on a bounded feasible set.
